overview.body:
**Avalokiteśvara** ​(*avalokiteshvara*) — ‌Compassion, ‌Mercy, Bodhisattva ​· ​Lord who ​looks ​down ​in compassion ‌— ​belongs to ​the ‌Buddhist tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ​"Compassion, Mercy, ​Bodhisattva". ​The name ​means ‌"Lord ​who looks ‌down ​in compassion"[^1].

‌**Avalokiteśvara** ​belongs to ‌the ​Buddhist tradition, ‌where ​it is ​associated ‌with compassion, ‌mercy, ‌bodhisattva.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores ​the ‌name as ​**Avalokiteśvara** ​and serves ‌its ​temple at ​[avalokiteshvara.com](https://punicodex.com/avalokiteshvara/). ‌The restoration ​preserves ‌at least ​one ​distinctive feature ​— ​a diacritic ‌or ‌a ​distinctive letter ‌— ​that the ​ASCII ‌form loses, ‌and ‌exactly one ‌historically ​valid Unicode ‌restoration ​exists, which ​places ​the name ‌in ​Tier ​1. The ​plain ‌ASCII form ​*avalokiteshvara* ​survives as ​a ‌modern convenience ​imposed ‌by the ​early ‌domain-name system; ​the ‌restoration, not ‌the ​fallback, ​is the ​form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^2].

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Devanagari as ‌**अवलोकितेश्वर**. Etymologically it ​means "Lord ​who looks down ​in compassion"[^1].

Sanskrit ​Avalokiteśvara, from ​avalokita 'beheld, looked ‌down upon' + ​īśvara 'lord'; ​the bodhisattva of ‌compassion, source-form of ​Guānyīn and ‌Kannon.

The ASCII ​form *avalokiteshvara* survives ‌only because ​the early domain-name ​system could ​not carry diacritics; ​it is a ​technological compromise, ‌not an ancient ​spelling. The Unicode ‌restoration **Avalokiteśvara** ​recovers the full ‌diacritic detail of ​the scholarly ‌transliteration directly in ​the address bar. ‌The restoration ​preserves at least ​one distinctive feature ‌— a ‌diacritic or a ‌distinctive letter ​— that the ​ASCII form loses, ‌and exactly ​one historically valid ​Unicode restoration exists, ‌which places ​the name in ​Tier 1.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- **a** ‌→ **A** — ​Same, capitalized
​- **v** → ​**v** — Same
​- **a** ‌→ **a** — ‌Same
- **l** ​→ **l** ‌— Same
- ​**o** → ​**o** — Same
‌- **k** → ‌**k** — ‌Same
- **i** ‌→ **i** — ​Same
- ‌**t** → **t** ​— Same
- ​**e** → ​**e** — Same
‌- **s** → ​**ś** — ​Ś: palatal sibilant, ​atomic letter (IAST ‌ś)
- ​**h** → **—** ​— Not ​written: sh digraph ‌realized as single ​letter ś
‌- **v** → ​**v** — Same
‌- **a** ​→ **a** — ‌Same
- **r** ‌→ **r** ​— Same
- ​**a** → **a** ​— Same

​The canonical temple ‌for this name ‌is served ​at **avalokiteshvara.com**[^2].

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the ​name is ​**/avalokiteshvara/** ​— ​Buddhist ‌Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

​- ‌**A** ​— Initial ‌character ​of ​the ​restored ​form ​Avalokiteśvara.
‌- ​**valokiteśvara** ‌— Remainder ​of ‌the ​name, ‌preserving ​the ‌distinctive ​marks ​of ‌the ‌Buddhist tradition.

‌For ​the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: ​'AVALOKITESHVARA' ‌— pronounce ​the ‌restored ​form ​with ​attention ​to ‌the ‌preserved ​diacritics ‌and length.

​Kindred ​and ‌historical ‌forms ‌of ‌the ​name:

‌- ​**Buddhist** ​— Avalokiteśvara, ​the ‌restored ​Unicode ​form ​of ‌the ​name

​Avalokiteśvara ​is Tier ‌1 ​because ‌the ​Buddhist ‌form ​preserves ‌distinctive ‌features ​that ​ASCII loses: ​stress, ​length, ‌or ‌special ​characters.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌**Avalokiteśvara** ‌circulate within ​the ​Buddhist corpus, ​where ​the figure ​embodies ‌compassion, mercy, ​bodhisattva.[^1]

​### Primary ‌Attestation ​(Sources)

Avalokiteśvara ‌is ​attested in ‌the ​canonical Buddhist ​sources ​as a ​figure ​associated with ‌compassion, mercy, ​bodhisattva.[^1]

‌### Name ​and ‌Meaning (Etymology)

​The ‌name means ​"Lord ‌who looks ​down ​in compassion" ‌and ‌reflects the ‌figure's ​role in ​the ‌tradition. **Avalokiteśvara** ​is ​the bodhisattva ‌of ​compassion who ​hears ‌the cries ​of ‌all sentient ​beings. ​In Mahāyāna ​sutras ​he descends ‌into ‌every realm ​to ‌save the ​suffering, ​manifesting in ‌forms ‌appropriate to ‌those ‌he teaches.[^1] ​In ‌East Asia ​he ​became the ​goddess ‌Guānyīn, while ​in Tibet ​he ​is the ‌patron ​bodhisattva manifesting ​through ​the Dalai ‌Lamas. ​The *Heart ‌Sūtra* ​and *Lotus ‌Sūtra* ​celebrate his ‌willingness ‌to assume ​any ​form—male, female, ​monarch, ​or beggar—to ‌liberate ‌beings from ​suffering.[^1]
